recipes.title: Build an MCP agent with no API key in 5 minutes
recipes.description: Import a ready MCP agent that runs on a fresh L2M install with a built-in echo model and a mock MCP server, then swap in a real model and server.
recipes.whatYouGet: One agent with a chat model and two MCP tools, a clock and a calculator, that runs on a fresh install.
recipes.summary: A manual trigger starts one Agent Orchestrator node. Its chat model is the built-in echo provider, and its tools come from the mock MCP server that runs inside L2M: `get_current_time` and `calculator`. Nothing needs a key, a network connection or a separate server. Echo is not a real model: it repeats the prompt back and never asks for a tool, so a local run makes one model call and ends. That proves the wiring works. To see the agent call tools, attach a real chat model.
steps:
Click **Run** in the editor, or call the run API with your own question. The API takes an API key from **Settings → Account → API Keys**:

   ```bash
   curl -X POST http://localhost:4000/api/workflows/wf-mcp-agent-quickstart/execute \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $L2M_API_KEY" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"user_prompt": "What is 2340 * 0.17?"}'
   ```
Open the run in the execution history and click the **Agent** node to read its trace.
Then change one thing at a time (see below).

sections.heading: What a run does
sections.body: We imported the file into a fresh install and ran it with the question above. The run succeeded in well under a second: - The **Agent** made one model call. The model was offered the two tools as `mock-mcp__get_current_time` and `mock-mcp__calculator`; L2M also adds a short note to the system prompt about its built-in `session_cache_list`, `session_cache_get` and `agent_clarify` tools. - Echo answered `Echo: What is 2340 * 0.17?`. The agent stopped after 1 iteration with `stopReason: "final_answer"`, and the **Output** node returned that text as `result`. - The two MCP Tool nodes are marked as used by the agent: they supplied the tool definitions. No tool ran, because echo asked for none. An empty question fails the run: the agent's user prompt template is `{{user_prompt}}`, and with nothing in it the Agent stops with "Agent Orchestrator user prompt is empty after template rendering".

sections.heading: See the loop with tool calls
sections.body: The demo's copy of this workflow plays an echo run too, so it shows no tool calls either. The demo's **Support agent** workflow plays a run recorded with a scripted stand-in model, so the demo needs no key. In that run the agent calls a knowledge-base tool once and a calculator tool twice before it answers: open it in the demo.

recipes.makeItYours:
- Replace the echo chat model node with a real one (OpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint) on the agent's `chat_model` port. A model that supports tool calling can then call the clock and the calculator.
- Replace the mock MCP tools with a server from your [MCP server registry](/product/mcp-server-registry), such as a filesystem or database server.
- Write your own system prompt on the agent node, and raise `maxIterations` (4 in the sample) only if the task needs more steps.
recipes.makeItSafer:
- `calculator` has no read-only annotation, so L2M counts it as a write tool. Turn on the workflow's **No write tools** setting and it is blocked for the agent, while the clock stays. See [MCP tool policy](/product/mcp-tool-policy#no-write-tools).
- Require a person's approval before write tools run: see [human approval for agent tool calls](/guides/human-approval-for-agent-tool-calls).
- Cap model spend with a [budget](/product/budgets).

recipes.title: Webhook to AI agent with memory and MCP tools
recipes.description: Trigger an agent from a webhook, give it session memory and MCP tools, and secure the webhook with a bearer token or HMAC signature.
recipes.keysNote: None: runs on the built-in Echo model; a real model to see tool calls
recipes.whatYouGet: An agent behind a webhook URL, with per-session memory and two MCP tools, that any app can call with a question and a session id.
recipes.summary: A **Webhook Input** node at `POST /webhook/agent-demo` passes `system_prompt`, `user_prompt` and `session_id` from the request body to an Agent Orchestrator. The agent has a chat model, a **Simple Memory** node keyed by the session id, and two tools from the mock MCP server built into L2M. As shipped, the chat model is the built-in Echo model, so the workflow runs with no key and no model server; Echo never calls tools, so attach a real model to see tool calls. As shipped, the webhook also has no authentication: secure it before you expose it.
steps: To try the webhook and memory, keep the built-in Echo model. For real answers and tool calls, open the chat model node, pick a provider in the **Provider** list (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Azure OpenAI, an OpenAI-compatible server or Ollama), set the model and, for a hosted provider, its key, then save. **Load models** lists the models the provider offers. For Ollama in Docker, `localhost` is the container: use `http://host.docker.internal:11434/v1` for Ollama on the host (on Linux, add `extra_hosts: ["host.docker.internal:host-gateway"]` to the `api` service).

Send a request:

   ```bash
   curl -X POST http://localhost:4000/webhook/agent-demo \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"system_prompt": "You are a helpful assistant.", "user_prompt": "What is 12 * 7?", "session_id": "demo-2"}'
   ```
Send a second request with the same `session_id` and a follow-up question. The agent now sees the first exchange.
Before anyone else can reach the URL, secure it (see below).

sections.heading: What a run does
sections.body:
Two things are worth knowing before you call it from an app.

**A model error comes back as the answer.** If the chat model call fails (the model is not pulled, the server is down, the key is wrong), the agent usually does not fail the run. It returns the error message as its answer, such as `Provider ollama request failed (404): ...`, with `stopReason: "error"`, and the webhook replies with that text in `output.result`. If an app gets text like that back, open the run and look at the Agent node.

**Memory, checked with the echo model.** The shipped chat model is the built-in echo provider. Two requests with `session_id: "demo-2"` returned `Echo: What is 12 * 7?` and then `Echo: And what time is it in Toronto?`. The second run's agent messages held the first question and answer before the new question: that is the memory. Echo never calls tools, so this check says nothing about tool use; a model that supports tool calling can call `get_current_time` and `calculator`.

Memory keeps the last 20 messages of a session (`maxMessages`) and, with **Persist Tool Messages** off, leaves tool results out of it. The tools' connection names an HTTP endpoint (`http://127.0.0.1:7001/mcp`), but the `mock-mcp` server runs inside L2M: nothing has to listen on that port.

sections.heading: Secure the webhook
sections.body:
With no auth mode set, anyone who can reach your L2M can call the agent and spend your model budget. On the Webhook Input node:

- **Bearer token.** Set the auth mode to `bearer_token`, the auth header name to `authorization`, and pick a stored secret that holds the token. Callers then send `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. We checked: without the header the call gets `401 {"error":"Unauthorized webhook request"}`; with it, the agent answers.
- **HMAC signature.** For callers that can sign requests, `hmac_sha256` checks a hex HMAC-SHA256 of `timestamp + "." + raw body`, sent with a timestamp header. Requests outside the replay window (300 seconds by default) and repeated signatures are rejected.
- **Idempotency.** Turn it on so a retried request with the same `Idempotency-Key` returns the first result instead of running the agent again; the same key with a different body gets `409`. Once it is on, every request must send the header, or it gets `400`.
- **Allowed addresses.** List the IPs or CIDR ranges that may call the trigger.

See [Secure webhooks](/security/secure-webhooks) for the signing format and error codes.

recipes.makeItYours:
- Switch the chat model to OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, with its key stored as a [secret](/security/secrets).
- Replace the mock tools with a server from your [MCP server registry](/product/mcp-server-registry).
- Raise `maxMessages` on the memory node for longer conversations, or lower it to keep prompts small.
recipes.makeItSafer:
- The sample takes `system_prompt` from the request, so any caller can rewrite the agent's instructions. Write the system prompt on the agent node instead.
- Require approval before write tools: with **Ask before write tools** on, the agent pauses before both `calculator` and `get_current_time`. This gate ignores the server's own read-only annotation and trusts only an admin's read-only mark on a registered server; the sample's inline mock tools are not registered, so both always pause. See [human approval for agent tool calls](/guides/human-approval-for-agent-tool-calls).
- Cap what callers can spend with a workflow [budget](/product/budgets).

recipes.title: Supervisor and worker agents: a runnable example
recipes.description: A supervisor agent hands work to a researcher and a calculator worker, each with its own tools. Imports and runs with no API key.
recipes.whatYouGet: A Supervisor agent with two worker agents, each with its own chat model and MCP tools, that runs on a fresh install.
recipes.summary: A Supervisor node coordinates two worker agents. The researcher has an MCP knowledge-base lookup tool; the computer has a calculator and a clock. The Supervisor sees each worker as one tool and decides which to call for each step, and each worker runs its own agent loop. Every agent uses the built-in echo provider and the mock MCP server built into L2M, so it runs with no API key. Echo never asks for a tool, so a local run shows the wiring, not the delegation: the Supervisor answers on its first turn and hands nothing off. Attach a real chat model to see it delegate.
recipes.makeItYours:
- Give each worker its own real chat model on its `chat_model` port: a small, cheap model often does for a narrow worker, while the Supervisor needs one that plans well.
- Swap a worker's mock tools for your own MCP servers.
- Add a third worker on the Supervisor's `worker` port when a new kind of task appears, rather than giving one agent every tool. Each worker adds a tool to the Supervisor's list and model calls to each run, so add one only for a distinct job.
recipes.makeItSafer:
- Keep write tools on one worker only, and require approval for them: see [human approval for agent tool calls](/guides/human-approval-for-agent-tool-calls).
- Record a good run as a [golden run](/product/golden-runs) and replay it after each change.

docs.text: Multi-agent systems: supervisor and worker agents

steps: Click **Run** in the editor, or call the run API with a question for the team (as in the [zero-key agent recipe](/recipes/zero-key-mcp-agent), with the workflow id `wf-supervisor-worker-swarm`).
Open the run and click the **Supervisor** node to read its trace.
Then change one thing at a time (see below).

sections.heading: What a run does
sections.body:
We ran the sample on a fresh install with "What is 17% of 2340, and what does MCP stand for?":

- The **Supervisor** made one model call and stopped after 1 iteration with `stopReason: "final_answer"`. Echo answered `Supervisor: What is 17% of 2340, and what does MCP stand for?`.
- Both workers, their chat models and their tools are marked **skipped** (`attachment_only_node`). Workers are not steps in the run: they run only when the Supervisor calls them, and echo never did.

The Supervisor is offered one tool per worker, named `delegate_to_` plus the worker's name with every character other than letters, digits, `_` and `-` turned into `_`: here `delegate_to_Worker__Researcher` and `delegate_to_Worker__Computer`. Each tool's description starts with "Delegate task to" and the worker's name, followed by the start of the worker's system prompt as a hint. Name workers so the Supervisor's model can tell them apart; two workers with the same name make the run fail.

sections.heading: See delegation in a recorded run
sections.body: The demo's **Research swarm** workflow is the same pattern with a researcher and an analyst, recorded with a scripted stand-in model, so it shows the delegation without a key. In its run the Supervisor calls `delegate_to_researcher`, then `delegate_to_analyst`, then writes the team summary: three iterations. Play it in the demo.

recipes.title: Serve an L2M workflow as an MCP tool
recipes.description: Turn a whole workflow into one MCP tool that agents and IDE clients can call, then serve it from a toolset with its own client token on the MCP gateway.
recipes.whatYouGet: A workflow that any MCP client can list and call as one tool, `answer_from_kb`, through L2M's MCP gateway.
recipes.summary: An **Expose as MCP Tool** trigger turns the workflow into a tool named `answer_from_kb`, with one required argument, `question`. Inside, an agent with the echo model and the mock `lookup_kb` tool answers it. Put the workflow in a toolset on the [MCP gateway](/product/mcp-gateway) and any MCP client holding a client token can list the tool and call it; each call runs the whole workflow. It runs with no API key. With echo, the answer is the question repeated back.
steps: As an admin, open **MCP → Toolsets** in the sidebar, create a toolset and add the workflow. Its endpoint is `/mcp/<slug>` (we named ours `kb-helper`).
Open **MCP → Clients**, create a client for that toolset (admin; you may be asked to confirm your identity again) and copy its token. It is shown once.
Call the tool with curl (below), or paste the client's configuration snippet into your MCP client.

sections.heading: Call it with curl
sections.body:
The gateway speaks MCP over Streamable HTTP. Put the client token in `TOKEN` (`export TOKEN=l2m_mcp_...`), then run these in order:

```bash
# 1. Open a session and keep the Mcp-Session-Id header the server sends back.
SESSION=$(curl -si http://localhost:4000/mcp/kb-helper \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"initialize","params":{"protocolVersion":"2025-11-25","capabilities":{},"clientInfo":{"name":"curl","version":"1"}}}' \
  | awk 'tolower($1)=="mcp-session-id:" {print $2}' | tr -d '\r')

# Tell the server the client is ready, as the MCP spec asks.
curl http://localhost:4000/mcp/kb-helper \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -H "Mcp-Session-Id: $SESSION" \
  -H "MCP-Protocol-Version: 2025-11-25" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","method":"notifications/initialized"}'

# 2. Call the tool in that session. (List them first with the same request and
#    "method":"tools/list", "params":{}.)
curl http://localhost:4000/mcp/kb-helper \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Accept: application/json, text/event-stream" \
  -H "Mcp-Session-Id: $SESSION" \
  -H "MCP-Protocol-Version: 2025-11-25" \
  -d '{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":3,"method":"tools/call","params":{"name":"answer_from_kb","arguments":{"question":"What is MCP?"}}}'

# 3. End the session.
curl -X DELETE http://localhost:4000/mcp/kb-helper \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Mcp-Session-Id: $SESSION"
```

What came back on our install:

- `initialize`: HTTP 200 with an `mcp-session-id` header and `{"protocolVersion":"2025-11-25","capabilities":{"tools":{"listChanged":false}},"serverInfo":{"name":"l2m-kb-helper","title":"KB helper",...}}`.
- `tools/list`: one tool, `answer_from_kb`, with the description and input schema from the trigger.
- `tools/call`: `content` with the workflow output as JSON text, the same object as `structuredContent` (`{"result":"Echo: What is MCP?"}`), and the run's id in `_meta.executionId`.
- `DELETE`: `204 No Content`.

Each call is a full run, listed in the execution history with the trigger type `mcp_gateway`. The gateway speaks MCP protocol versions 2025-11-25, 2025-06-18 and 2025-03-26. An MCP client library or app does these steps for you.

sections.heading: The sample's legacy routes are public
sections.body: The trigger also has a `path` (`kb-helper`) and `authMode: "public"`, which serve the older REST routes `GET /api/mcp-server/kb-helper/manifest` and `POST /api/mcp-server/kb-helper/invoke`. On our install both answered without any credentials, and `invoke` ran the workflow. They are not MCP, so MCP clients do not need them: set the trigger's auth mode to `bearer` with a stored secret, or remove the `path`, before you deploy. See [Expose a workflow as an MCP tool](/runtime/workflow-as-mcp-tool#legacy-rest-routes).

recipes.makeItYours:
- Change `toolName`, `toolDescription` and `inputSchema` on the trigger. The description is what other agents' models read to decide when to call your tool, so make it specific.
- Replace the agent's echo model with a real one, or replace the agent with a retrieval step and an LLM call, as in the [RAG knowledge base recipe](/recipes/rag-knowledge-base).
- Call it from another L2M instance: register `https://<l2m-host>/mcp/<slug>` there with the `http_mcp` adapter and the client token as a stored secret.
recipes.makeItSafer:
- Give each client only the toolsets it needs, the lowest role that works, and an expiry.
- Add [tool policy](/product/mcp-tool-policy) rules scoped to the client or the toolset, including require-approval rules.
- Cap each client with a [budget](/product/budgets) scoped to **MCP client** and a rate limit on the client.

recipes.title: RAG with a built-in knowledge base, no vector DB
recipes.description: Ingest documents into L2M's built-in knowledge base and answer questions from them, with no external vector database and no API key to start.
recipes.whatYouGet: A question-answering workflow that retrieves from a knowledge base stored in L2M's own database, with no vector database and no API key.
recipes.summary: A **Question** node holds the question. **RAG Retrieve** searches a built-in knowledge base for the three nearest chunks, a **Prompt Template** puts them into a grounded prompt, and an **LLM** node answers. The sample uses `token-embedder`, a hash-based demo embedder that needs no key (its search quality is poor), and the echo model. Echo returns the prompt it was given, which is useful here: the answer shows exactly what a real model would read. Swap both for real ones to get real answers.
steps: As an admin, create a knowledge base with the `token-embedder` and add a document, under **Knowledge** in the sidebar or with the API (below). Get its id (`kb_...`) from the create response or from `GET /api/knowledge-bases`; the Knowledge page does not show it.
Open the **RAG Retrieve (KB)** node and replace `<your-kb-id>` with that id. Save.
Run it, then change the question on the **Question** node and run it again.

sections.heading: Create a knowledge base with the API
sections.body:
```bash
# An admin's API key, from Settings → Account → API Keys.
export L2M_API_KEY=ao_...

# Create a knowledge base. The response holds its id: kb_...
curl -X POST http://localhost:4000/api/knowledge-bases \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $L2M_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "Helpdesk FAQ", "embedderId": "token-embedder", "embedderConfig": {}}'

# Load, chunk, embed and store a Markdown file in one call.
export KB_ID=kb_...   # the id from the response above
curl -X POST http://localhost:4000/api/knowledge-bases/$KB_ID/upload \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $L2M_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"filename": "helpdesk-faq.md", "sourceId": "helpdesk-faq-v1",
       "content": "# Helpdesk FAQ\n\n## Reset your password\nTo reset your password, open the sign-in page, choose Forgot password, and enter your work email. The reset link is valid for 30 minutes.\n\n## Change your billing plan\nAdmins can change the billing plan under Settings, then Billing. Changes apply from the next invoice.\n\n## Export your data\nGo to Settings, then Data, and choose Export. You get a ZIP file with one CSV per table.",
       "chunking": {"strategy": "recursive", "chunkSize": 300, "chunkOverlap": 0}}'
```

On our install the upload answered `{"sourceId":"helpdesk-faq-v1","documentsLoaded":1,"chunksInserted":2,"dimensions":64}`. The embedder you create the knowledge base with must match the `embedderId` on the RAG Retrieve node, or the question and the chunks are not compared in the same space.

sections.heading: What a run does
sections.body:
We ran the sample on a fresh install, against a knowledge base holding a short helpdesk FAQ (a password-reset section, a billing section and a data-export section, stored as 2 chunks):

- **RAG Retrieve** returned both chunks, the password-reset chunk first (similarity 0.375, against 0.131 for the other), each with its `chunkId`, `sourceId` and score.
- **Grounded Prompt** numbered them `[1]` and `[2]` under "Context:" and added the question.
- **LLM** (echo) returned that whole prompt, prefixed with `Echo: `, and **Output** returned it as `result`.

Two things to know:

- **A missing id fails quietly.** Run the sample without replacing `<your-kb-id>` and it still succeeds: retrieval returns no documents and the prompt's context is empty. If answers look ungrounded, check the retrieve node's `documents` first.
- **The template asks for chunk ids, but the context shows numbers.** The prompt says "Cite the chunkId for every claim" while the context lists `[1]`, `[2]`. For citations that resolve to their sources, use the `citationInstructions` the retrieve node emits and the citation tools in [Knowledge bases](/nodes/knowledge-bases#citations-phase-9-4).

sections.heading: Variant: retrieve from a connector
sections.body: [`rag-flow.json`](https://github.com/TensorGreed/ai-orchestrator/blob/main/samples/workflows/rag-flow.json) loads documents from a **Connector Source** (Google Drive) on every run and retrieves from them in memory, with no knowledge base. As shipped it runs on the built-in echo model. We ran it that way with no Google credentials: the connector ran in demo-fallback mode and returned five built-in sample documents, and retrieval put the three closest to "How does MCP fit into an AI workflow builder?" into the prompt. Use a knowledge base when the documents should be ingested once and kept; use a connector for small sets that change between runs.

recipes.makeItYours:
- Use a real embedder (for example `openai-embedder`, with its key as a [secret](/security/secrets)) for the knowledge base and the same `embedderId` on the node. A knowledge base keeps the vector size of its first chunks, so start a new one when you change embedders.
- Replace the echo model with a real one on the **LLM** node.
- Set `searchMode` to `hybrid` to add keyword (BM25) matches to vector search, and add a **Rerank** node for better ordering. See [hybrid search](/nodes/knowledge-bases#hybrid-search-phase-9-3).
recipes.makeItSafer:
- Retrieved documents are outside content: a document can carry instructions for the model. [Content rules](/product/content-rules#outside-content-at-the-model-boundary) can check each retrieved document before it reaches the model.
- Cap model spend with a [budget](/product/budgets) once you switch to a paid model.

recipes.title: Let an AI agent ask a clarifying question
recipes.description: A chat agent that pauses to ask the user a question when a request is ambiguous, then picks up where it stopped when the user replies.
recipes.keysNote: OpenAI API key, or any model with tool calling
recipes.whatYouGet: A chat agent that asks one focused question instead of guessing, and carries on with the answer.
recipes.summary: A **Chat** trigger sends each message to one Agent Orchestrator with a chat model and session memory. Every agent in L2M has a built-in tool, `agent_clarify`, that the model can call when it cannot finish without something only the user knows. The agent then stops with the question as its answer, and the chat shows it as a question. The user's next message in the same session goes back to the agent as the answer to that question, and the agent carries on. The sample's system prompt tells the model to ask only when the ambiguity changes the answer. As shipped, the chat model is OpenAI `gpt-4o-mini`; any chat model that supports tool calling works.
steps: Open the **GPT-4o-mini** chat model node and pick a stored secret that holds your OpenAI API key (or set `OPENAI_API_KEY` on the API server). Save the node and the workflow. Without a key the run fails with `Chat model node "GPT-4o-mini" (model_1) has no OpenAI API key`. To use another model, replace the node with any chat model node on the agent's `chat_model` port.
On the **Workflows** page, open the workflow's menu and choose **Chat**.
Send a request that is missing something, such as "Book me a table for Friday". If the model decides to ask, the reply bubble is labelled **Assistant is asking**.
Answer in the same chat. The agent resumes with your answer and replies normally.

sections.heading: How agent_clarify pauses a run
How the reply resumes it
sections.body:
There is no special resume call. The next run with the same `session_id` and a non-empty message loads session memory, finds the unanswered `agent_clarify` call at the end, and hands the new message to the model as that call's result, `{"ok":true,"output":{"user_reply":"..."}}`, instead of as a new user message. Model APIs expect every tool call to be followed by its result, so the conversation stays valid and the model reads the reply as the answer to its own question.

Memory normally leaves tool results out (the sample's memory node keeps the default), but `agent_clarify` results are always saved. Without that, the next message would find the old question still open and be treated as another answer.

In the studio's chat, every message in a chat session sends the same `session_id`, so this happens by itself. A webhook or API caller does the same thing by hand: when the result has `clarification`, show the question, then call the workflow again with the same `session_id` and the user's reply as `user_prompt`.

sections.heading: What a run does
sections.body:
We ran the sample on a fresh install without a model key, in two ways.

**With the echo provider.** Echo repeats the prompt and never calls a tool, so it never asks. `Book me a table for Friday` came back as `Echo: Book me a table for Friday` with `stopReason: "final_answer"` after one model call. A second message in the same session showed the first exchange in the agent's messages: memory works, but this says nothing about the question itself.

**With a scripted stand-in model.** To watch the pause and the resume, we pointed the chat model at a small local OpenAI-compatible server that answers the first message with an `agent_clarify` call and answers a tool result with text. The model was offered `session_cache_list`, `session_cache_get` and `agent_clarify`. Then:

- Run 1, `Book me a table for Friday`: the agent stopped after 1 iteration with `stopReason: "clarification_requested"`. Output `result` was `Which restaurant, and for how many people?`, and the run result carried `clarification` with that question, the reason `The booking depends on both.`, the tool call id and `nodeId: "agent_1"`.
- Run 2, same session, `Luigi's, four people`: the model received no new user message. Its last message was the tool result `{"ok":true,"output":{"user_reply":"Luigi's, four people"}}` for the same call id, and the agent ended normally with `stopReason: "final_answer"`.

The scripted server shows the mechanism, not judgment: whether a real model asks, and when, depends on the model and the prompt. The demo has no copy of this workflow.

sections.heading: Ask or guess?
sections.body: A question costs the user a turn, so ask only when the answer would change what the agent does: "email him" with no name, "the report" when there are three. Let the agent infer what it reasonably can, and do not use the clarify tool as a confirmation step. A clarifying question is not an approval either: nobody approves anything, and the reply is just more input. To make a person approve an action before it runs, use [human approval for agent tool calls](/guides/human-approval-for-agent-tool-calls). [Human in the loop](/learn/agents/human-in-the-loop) compares the two.

recipes.makeItYours:
- Attach MCP tools on the agent's `tool` port. The agent can then look things up first and ask only about what the tools cannot answer.
- Tune the system prompt: name the details that are worth a question in your domain (a customer id, a date range) and the ones the agent should assume.
- Call it from your own app: put a [Webhook Input](/nodes/reference/input) trigger in place of the Chat trigger, pass `user_prompt` and `session_id`, and check the result for `clarification`.
recipes.makeItSafer:
- Cap model spend per workflow with a [budget](/product/budgets).
- Keep `maxIterations` low (5 in the sample) so a confused agent stops early.
- When you add tools that change things, require a person's approval before they run: see [human approval for agent tool calls](/guides/human-approval-for-agent-tool-calls).

recipes.title: Extract a brand's name, logo and colors from a website
recipes.description: Load a web page in headless Chromium, then have an LLM return the brand name, logo URL, colors, font and tagline as JSON. A small web-to-data workflow.
recipes.keysNote: OpenAI API key and Playwright Chromium
recipes.whatYouGet: A workflow that turns a website URL into one JSON object: brand name, logo URL, primary and accent color, font and tagline.
recipes.summary: A **Text Input** holds the URL (`https://example.com` as shipped). **Web Browse** opens it in headless Chromium, waits for the network to go quiet, and extracts the title, text, meta tags, images and a screenshot. A **Prompt Template** puts the title, the description, Open Graph image and theme-color meta tags, the first 10 images and the first 4,000 characters of text into an extraction prompt. An **LLM Call** answers it, an **Output Parser** checks the JSON, and the **Output** returns it. It needs an OpenAI key as shipped and Chromium for Playwright on the API host. Read [what the model really sees](#what-the-model-really-sees) before you rely on colors and fonts.
steps: Install Chromium for Playwright on the API host once: `pnpm exec playwright install chromium` from the repo root (Playwright itself comes with the workflow engine). Or point `PDF_CHROMIUM_EXECUTABLE_PATH` at a Chromium you already have.

Open the **LLM** node and pick a stored secret with your OpenAI API key under **API Key Secret** (or set `OPENAI_API_KEY` on the API server), or switch the provider. Save. Without a key the **LLM** node fails with `Provider openai requires an API key via secretRef or OPENAI_API_KEY`.

Run it. A `user_prompt` sent with the run replaces the Text Input's URL, so you can try other sites without editing the workflow. Put an API key from **Settings → Account → API Keys** in `L2M_API_KEY`:

   ```bash
   curl -X POST http://localhost:4000/api/workflows/wf-branding-extract-flow/execute \
     -H "Authorization: Bearer $L2M_API_KEY" \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"user_prompt": "https://www.wikipedia.org"}'
   ```
Open the run: **Parse JSON** holds the object, and the **Output** returns it as a JSON string in `result`.

sections.heading: Web Browse: pages that need JavaScript
sections.body:
A plain HTTP request gets the HTML a server sends. Many sites build the page in the browser, so that HTML is nearly empty. [Web Browse](/nodes/web-browse) loads the page in headless Chromium through Playwright, runs its scripts and reads the result. The sample waits for `networkidle`, allows 45 seconds, and uses a 1440 x 900 viewport. Besides the nested `brandSite` object, it puts `url`, `title`, `text`, `html`, `screenshot`, `meta`, `links` and `images` at the top level for the next node. Each call starts and closes its own browser, so keep it to low-volume flows.

Without Chromium the run fails at this node. We pointed `PDF_CHROMIUM_EXECUTABLE_PATH` at a missing file to check: **Fetch Brand Site** failed with `browserType.launch: Failed to launch chromium because executable doesn't exist at ...`, the later nodes were skipped, and the run ended with an error.

sections.heading: What a run does
sections.body:
We ran it with Chromium installed and no model key. On `https://example.com` the browse step took about 0.9 seconds and returned the title `Example Domain`, the page text and a screenshot, with no images and no Open Graph tags. On `https://www.wikipedia.org` it took about 1.5 seconds and found an `og:image`, a description and a list of image URLs, the Wikipedia logo first. The prompt then held the title, the description, the `og:image` URL, an empty theme color (the page sets none), the images and the first 4,000 of 4,077 characters of text.

- **With the echo provider**, the model only repeats the prompt, so there is nothing real to parse. The parser picked up the image list from the echoed prompt (see below), and the Output returned that list.
- **With a scripted stand-in model** that answers with one JSON object (the page title as `brand`, the `og:image` URL as the logo, empty colors and font), the parser accepted it on the first try, and the Output returned `{"brand":"Wikipedia","primaryLogoUrl":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/...","primaryColor":"",...}` as `result`.

The stand-in shows the plumbing. How well a real model fills in each field depends on the model and the page.

sections.heading: What the model really sees
sections.body: The prompt gives the model the page title, three meta tags (`description`, `og:image`, `theme-color`), up to 10 image URLs and up to 4,000 characters of visible text. It does not send the screenshot, the HTML or any CSS, so the model never sees a color or a font on the page. The prompt says so, and asks for a color or font only when the data states it, such as a `theme-color` meta tag, and an empty string otherwise. Expect empty colors on many sites. The brand name, the logo URL and the tagline come from real page data and are the reliable part. The template reads meta tags with `{{ meta["og:image"] }}`: a simple path such as `meta.og:image` cannot hold a colon, and would render empty. It trims lists with `{{ images.slice(0, 10) }}` and `{{ text.slice(0, 4000) }}`. The browse node keeps the screenshot in the run so you can check the page yourself; set `screenshot: false` if you do not need it.

sections.heading: Parsing and the final output
sections.body: The **Parse JSON** node runs in `json_schema` mode with `lenient` parsing: it reads the first JSON value it finds in the reply. The schema requires `brand` and `primaryLogoUrl`. If the value fails the check, the node asks the same model up to 2 more times to fix it, then fails. The checks apply only when the value is an object: an array passes as it is. That is how the echo run passed with the image list. A real model that follows the prompt returns one object, but if it adds a list before the object, the parser takes the list. Check `parserTrace` on the node when the result looks wrong. The **Output** node's response template is `{{parsed}}`, so the run returns the object as a JSON string in `result`.

sections.heading: Outbound URL checks
sections.body: The URL can come from whoever calls the workflow, so it is checked. Web Browse refuses `file:` URLs, and every request the page makes, including redirects and images, goes through L2M's [outbound URL checks](/security/outbound-url-checks): cloud metadata addresses and link-local ranges are always refused. Private ranges and localhost are allowed by default. Set `OUTBOUND_DENY_PRIVATE=true` if callers must not reach your internal network through this node. Page text is untrusted input: a page can carry instructions aimed at the model, so do not give this workflow tools that act on what a page says.

recipes.makeItYours: - Take the URL from a webhook: replace the Text Input with a [Webhook Input](/nodes/reference/input); the browse node's URL template is already `{{user_prompt}}`. - Set `screenshot: false` on the browse node: the prompt does not use it, and it adds a large base64 image to every run. - Feed the JSON to a report: the [PDF report with charts recipe](/recipes/pdf-report-with-charts) builds an HTML page and a PDF, and can take colors from here. - Swap OpenAI for another provider on the LLM node.
recipes.makeItSafer:
- Turn on `OUTBOUND_DENY_PRIVATE` and list the internal hosts you do want in `OUTBOUND_ALLOWLIST`: see [outbound URL checks](/security/outbound-url-checks#configuration).
- Cap model spend with a [budget](/product/budgets).
- Read [prompt injection](/learn/security/prompt-injection) before you add tools to any workflow that reads web pages.

recipes.title: Generate a PDF report with charts from data
recipes.description: Render Vega-Lite charts to SVG on the server, place them in an HTML template and print it to PDF with headless Chromium. No model and no API key needed.
recipes.keysNote: No API key; Playwright Chromium for the PDF
recipes.whatYouGet: A two-page A4 PDF with three charts (a bar chart, a donut and an ageing histogram), built from data in the workflow.
recipes.summary: A **Set** node holds three small data sets: key counts by cloud, by algorithm and by age. Three **Chart** nodes turn them into SVG from [Vega-Lite](https://vega.github.io/vega-lite/) specs, on the server, with no browser. A **Prompt Template** places the SVGs in an HTML page, and **PDF Output** prints that page to A4 with headless Chromium. No model is involved, so it runs without a key. Swap the Set node for real data, such as an HTTP request, a database query or an MCP tool, and the rest stays the same.
steps: Install Chromium for Playwright on the API host once: `pnpm exec playwright install chromium` from the repo root. Or point `PDF_CHROMIUM_EXECUTABLE_PATH` at a Chromium you already have.
Run it. Open the run and click **PDF**: the node output has the file as `pdf.downloadUrl` (a `data:application/pdf;base64,...` URL) and `pdf.base64`. The **Output** node returns that URL as `result`.
Save the PDF from the URL, or run the workflow from the studio's chat, which shows a **Download PDF** link when the answer is a PDF data URL.

sections.heading: What a run does
sections.body: On our install the whole run took about 1.2 seconds. The three charts took 10 to 30 ms each, and the PDF step about 1.1 seconds, most of it starting Chromium. The PDF was 34,859 bytes, two A4 pages titled `Key Inventory Report`: the cloud bar chart and the algorithm donut on page 1, and the age histogram on page 2, below a heading left at the foot of page 1. Add `h2{break-after:avoid}.chart{break-inside:avoid}` to the template's CSS to keep each heading with its chart. The file name came out as `key-report-.pdf`: its template is `key-report-{{session_id}}.pdf` and a run without a session has an empty `session_id`. Pass a `session_id`, or use another value in the name. **Without Chromium.** We pointed `PDF_CHROMIUM_EXECUTABLE_PATH` at a missing file. The three charts and the HTML still rendered, then the **PDF** node failed with `browserType.launch: Failed to launch chromium because executable doesn't exist at ...` and the run ended with an error. Chart rendering never needs the browser; only the HTML-to-PDF step does.

sections.heading: The chart specs
sections.body: Each Chart node holds a Vega-Lite spec without data. Vega-Lite describes a chart as a `mark` (bar, arc, line...) and an `encoding` that maps data fields to channels such as `x`, `y`, `theta` and `color`. The node's `dataPath` (`byCloud`, `byAlgorithm`, `ageing`) points at rows from the earlier node and fills in the data. The Set node's values are JSON strings, and the run turned them into arrays of rows. The age chart sets `"sort": null` on its x axis so the buckets keep their order (`<30d`, `30-90d` and so on) instead of sorting by name. `width` and `height` on the node are defaults; a size in the spec wins. Each chart's `outputKey` (`cloudChart` and so on) holds `svg` and a `dataUrl`. The node also puts `svg`, `dataUrl` and a ready `imgTag` at the top level, but three charts feed one template here and those top-level keys overwrite each other, so the template uses `{{cloudChart.svg}}` to inline each SVG. See the [Chart node](/nodes/chart) for every field, and use `specTemplate` when the spec itself depends on the data.

sections.heading: HTML template and PDF output
sections.body:
The **HTML Report** node is a Prompt Template used as an HTML template: a full page with inline CSS and the three SVGs. Nothing in it calls a model. **PDF Output** in `html` render mode reads the `html` key, loads it in Chromium, waits for the network to go quiet (up to 45 seconds) and prints with `printBackground` on and the `A4` page size (`Letter`, `Legal`, `A3` and `A5` also work).

Anything the HTML loads from the web, such as a font or an image URL, goes through the [outbound URL checks](/security/outbound-url-checks). The inline SVGs load nothing. PDF Output also has a `text` mode that writes plain text into a PDF without a browser, but it cannot show charts.

sections.heading: Add an LLM summary (optional)
sections.body: To open the report with a written summary, add a Prompt Template after **Sample Data** that asks for a short summary of the rows (for example with `{{byCloud}}` and `{{ageing}}`), then an LLM Call, and connect the LLM Call to **HTML Report** next to the charts. Then put its answer into the template as `{{answer}}`. The model only writes text; the numbers in the charts still come from the data.

recipes.makeItYours:
- Replace **Sample Data** with real data: an [HTTP Request](/nodes/reference/connector), a database connector or an MCP tool, as long as the rows reach the charts under the names in `dataPath`. The [branded PDF inventory report](/recipes/key-inventory-pdf-report) does this with an MCP tool and a Python step.
- Brand it: change the colors in the specs (`mark.color`, `scale.scheme`), or pass a Vega `theme` object on each Chart node so every chart shares one style. The [brand extraction recipe](/recipes/brand-extraction-web) finds a site's logo and colors.
- Run it on a schedule with a Schedule Trigger and send the PDF on with an email or storage node.
recipes.makeItSafer:
- If any HTML comes from user input or a model, turn on `OUTBOUND_DENY_PRIVATE` (off by default) so the page cannot load internal URLs: see [outbound URL checks](/security/outbound-url-checks#configuration).
- The PDF travels as base64 inside the run result and is stored with the run, so anyone who can read the run can read the report.

recipes.title: A coding agent in VS Code backed by your own workflow
recipes.description: Connect the L2M VS Code extension to a workflow that returns chat, code blocks, patch previews and commands that run only after you approve them.
recipes.keysNote: A model (local Ollama as shipped) and the VS Code extension
recipes.whatYouGet: A chat panel in VS Code whose answers come from an L2M workflow you can edit: code blocks, file patches you preview and apply, and commands you approve.
recipes.summary: The L2M VS Code extension sends each chat message, with a bounded bundle of workspace context, to an L2M workflow. This workflow is the server side: a **Webhook Input** with the path `vscode-l2m-agent`, an Agent Orchestrator with a chat model and session memory, an **Output Parser** that checks the reply against a JSON contract, and an **Output**. The extension turns the reply into chat text, code blocks and actions. It changes files or runs commands only after you approve each one in a modal dialog. The model and the prompt live in the workflow, so you can switch models without touching the editor. As shipped, the chat model is `qwen2.5:7b` on a local Ollama server.
steps: Point the **Chat Model** node at a model you have: pull `qwen2.5:7b` into Ollama, or switch the provider to OpenAI, Anthropic or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint with its key as a stored secret. A larger model follows the JSON contract more reliably. Save.
Create an API key in **Settings → Account → API Keys** (a builder role or above can run workflows). It is shown once.

Install the extension. Build the `.vsix` from `apps/vscode-l2m-agent` or take it from a CI run, then `code --install-extension vscode-l2m-agent.vsix`. See [VS Code extension](/getting-started/vscode-extension#install-development-build).

In VS Code settings, set `l2mAgent.apiBaseUrl` (default `http://localhost:4000`), `l2mAgent.workflowId` to `wf-vscode-l2m-coding-agent` (or leave it empty to find the workflow by its webhook path), and `l2mAgent.authToken` to the key. Put the key in your user settings, not in a workspace `settings.json` that might be committed.
Open **L2M Agent** in the Activity Bar and ask for a change in the open file.

sections.heading: The request and the contract
sections.body:
The extension calls `POST /api/webhooks/execute/stream` (or `/api/webhooks/execute` with streaming off) with the API key as a bearer token. The body has `user_prompt`, `session_id`, its own `system_prompt`, and `variables` with the workspace context: the active file and selection, open editors, diagnostics, git status and diffs, pinned files, the extension's compacted memory, recent turns, and `actionResults`, which says which earlier patches and commands you approved. The [settings](/getting-started/vscode-extension#context-budget-tuning) cap each part, for example 12,000 characters per file and 60,000 in all.

The agent's system prompt asks for exactly one JSON object: `status` (`complete` or `needs_more_info`), `message`, `actions` (patches with a single-file unified diff, or commands), `codes`, `attachments`, `context_update` and `follow_up_question`. It also says never to claim a change unless `actionResults` shows it was approved. **Contract Parser** checks the reply in `anything_goes` mode: the required top-level fields, the `status` values and the string fields' types, not the items inside the arrays. It asks the model once to fix a bad reply, and if that fails too it returns `parsed: null` with a warning instead of failing the run.

sections.heading: What a run does
sections.body:
We sent the extension's request shape to a fresh install with a request to add a docstring, without VS Code and without a model key.

**With the echo provider**, the agent echoed the prompt back, the parser found no `status` field even after one retry (`Output parsing failed: Missing required field: status`), and the workflow returned an empty `result`. The streaming route sent `execution_started`, `node_start`, `node_activity`, `node_complete` and a final `result` event.

**With a scripted stand-in model** that answers with a valid contract, the parser accepted it on the first try. The workflow returned the object as a JSON string in `result`, with a `patch` action for `src/math.py`, its unified diff, and a `context_update`. We did not drive the VS Code side; the rest of this page describes it from the extension's source.

sections.heading: Safety model
sections.body:
The extension, not the workflow, decides what touches your machine:

- **Patches.** **Preview** opens a diff view of the result before anything is written. **Apply** asks again in a modal dialog, then writes the file. A patch must be a single-file unified diff whose target matches the action's file. The path is resolved against the first workspace folder and refused if it ends up outside it, whether through `..` or an absolute path. The check works on the path text; it does not resolve symbolic links.
- **Commands.** **Preview** shows the command and its working directory. **Run** asks in a modal dialog, then types the command into a new VS Code terminal named **L2M Agent Action**, where you can watch it. The working directory must also be inside the workspace. The extension never runs a command on its own, and it asks for approval even when the workflow sets `requiresApproval: false`.
- **Results.** Each approval, rejection or failure is saved with the session and sent back in `actionResults` on the next request. A command's terminal output is not sent back.

The workflow sees only what the extension sends. The sample attaches no tools, so the agent cannot read other files or run anything itself. If you attach MCP tools, those run on the L2M server under your tool rules, outside this approval flow.

sections.heading: The webhook path is open as shipped
sections.body: The extension uses the signed-in `/api/webhooks/execute` routes: they check your API key and do not look at the node's auth settings. The **Webhook Input** node also serves `POST /webhook/vscode-l2m-agent`, and the sample sets no auth mode on it. On our install that URL ran the workflow with no credentials. If others can reach your L2M, open the node and set **Auth Mode** to **Bearer Token** or **HMAC SHA256**; the extension keeps working. Clearing the **Path** does not close the URL: an empty path falls back to the node id, so the workflow answers at `/webhook/webhook_1` instead. It also stops the extension from finding the workflow, unless `l2mAgent.workflowId` is set. See [Secure webhooks](/security/secure-webhooks#webhook-auth-modes).

recipes.makeItYours:
- Rewrite the system prompt for your stack: test commands, code style, the files that matter.
- Lower the context limits in the extension settings for small local models, or raise them for large-context models.
- Attach read-only MCP tools (a repository search, docs lookup) on the agent's `tool` port so it can look things up on the server.
- Each chat session sends its own `session_id`, and the workflow's memory keeps the last 24 messages of it (`maxMessages`); the extension also sends its own compacted memory.
recipes.makeItSafer:
- Set an auth mode on the Webhook Input (above), so its public URL does not run the workflow for anyone who can reach L2M.
- Give the extension a key of its own, so you can revoke it alone.
- Cap model spend with a [budget](/product/budgets).
- If you attach tools that change things, set [tool policy](/product/mcp-tool-policy) rules or require [approval](/guides/human-approval-for-agent-tool-calls) for them.

recipes.title: RAG with citations: answers that show their sources
recipes.description: Have the model mark each claim with [N], resolve every marker to the chunk and document it came from, and check that the cited sources back the claims.
recipes.keysNote: An OpenAI key as shipped; none with the demo embedder and echo
recipes.whatYouGet: A RAG workflow whose answer carries [1]-style markers, each resolved to the chunk id, source id and score of the document it cites.
recipes.summary: **Retrieve** runs a hybrid search over a built-in knowledge base and returns the four best chunks as numbered context. It also emits `citationInstructions`, a short instruction that tells the model to end each claim with the number of its source, such as `[2]`. The **Grounded Prompt** puts both into the prompt, the **LLM** answers, and **Extract Citations** finds every marker in the answer and maps it back to its chunk. As shipped, retrieval uses `openai-embedder` and the LLM uses `gpt-4o-mini`, both with the server's `OPENAI_API_KEY`. To try the wiring without a key, switch to the `token-embedder` demo embedder and the echo model.
steps: Create a knowledge base and add a document, as in the [knowledge base recipe](/recipes/rag-knowledge-base#create-a-knowledge-base-with-the-api). Create it with the embedder the **Retrieve** node uses: `openai-embedder` as shipped, or `token-embedder` to start with no key.

With no OpenAI key, use echo for the **LLM** node. The **Provider** list has no echo entry, so set the node's `providerId` to `echo` in the JSON file and import it again before you edit the nodes below.

Open **Retrieve** and replace `<your-kb-id>` with the knowledge base id, in **Vector Store Extra Config (JSON)**. If you used `token-embedder`, set **Embedder** to **Token Based (Local Demo)**. Leave **Vector Store** alone: its list has no entry for the built-in knowledge base, so it may show another store, but the saved `knowledge-base` value stays. Save.
Run it, then open the run and click **Extract Citations** to read the resolved citations.

sections.heading: What a run does
sections.body: We ran the sample on a fresh install against a knowledge base holding a short helpdesk FAQ in 4 chunks (password reset, billing, data export and an error code). **As shipped, with no OpenAI key**, the run stops at **Retrieve**: `OpenAI Embedding API error: Unauthorized`. The question has to be embedded before anything is searched. **With `token-embedder` and echo**, the run succeeded. Retrieve returned all 4 chunks, the password-reset chunk first, each with its `chunkId`, `sourceId`, `similarityScore` and `retrieval.mode: "hybrid"`. Echo answered with the whole prompt, so the answer contained `[1]` to `[4]` from the numbered context and `[1]`, `[2]` and `[3]` from the citation instructions' own examples. Extract Citations found 8 markers and `hasCitations: true`. That shows the plumbing, not a model citing: a check that only asks "are there citations?" passes a prompt echoed back. **With a scripted stand-in model.** To see real resolution without a provider key, we pointed the LLM node at a small local OpenAI-compatible server that returns a fixed answer: "Open the sign-in page, choose Forgot password and enter your work email [1]. The reset link is valid for 30 minutes [1]. If sign-in fails with E1042, your session expired: retry in a new tab [3]." Extract Citations returned 3 citations covering 2 documents (`uniqueCitedDocuments: 2`). Each one carries the marker, the 1-based `index`, the `chunkId`, `sourceId`, `knowledgeBaseId`, the chunk text, the score and the marker's `startIndex` and `endIndex` in the answer. An answer with no markers returned `hasCitations: false` and an empty list. A marker that matches no document, such as `[7]` with four documents, is skipped. The **Output** node returns only `{{answer}}`, the text with its markers. The citations stay in the Extract Citations output. The studio's chat panel reads them from there and shows each marker as a link to a footnote. An app calling the workflow through the API gets only the text unless you add `{{citations}}` to the Output template, which renders the list as JSON.

sections.heading: Check that the citations hold up
sections.body:
A citation proves which chunk the model pointed at, not that the chunk says what the model claims. To check that, add an **Output Guardrail** node after Extract Citations with the **Grounded in sources** check (`grounding`) and **On Fail** left at **Stop with Error**. It splits the answer into claims and looks for each claim's words in the documents it cites. See [grounding in sources](/product/content-rules-output-checks#grounding-in-sources).

We tried it with the stand-in model. The answer above passed. "The reset link is valid for 24 hours and arrives by text message [2]." failed the run with `Output guardrail checks failed: grounding (block: ungrounded (output.grounding))`, because document 2 is the billing chunk. An answer with no markers passed by default, since its words appear in the documents; with **Every claim must cite a source** (`requireCitations`) turned on, it failed too.

The check is lexical. It catches a claim that cites the wrong chunk or says something no chunk says. A paraphrase in new words can read as unsupported, and a changed figure inside an otherwise matching sentence can slip through. It is optional; simple workflows need none of it.

sections.heading: Score answers in evals
sections.body: To test a change to the prompt, the chunking or the embedder, run fixtures through the eval framework with the RAG scorers in [Knowledge bases](/nodes/knowledge-bases#rag-specific-eval-scorers-phase-9-5). `context_precision` and `context_recall` are programmatic and cost nothing per fixture. `faithfulness` and `answer_relevance` call a judge model with the server's provider keys, so they need both `EVAL_JUDGE_ENABLED=true` and `EVAL_JUDGE_ALLOW_ENV_CREDENTIALS=true`. The scorers read `documents` and `answer` from the run's output. This sample's output is only `result`, the answer text, so the context scorers find no chunks. In the copy you evaluate, delete the Output node: the run's output is then the Extract Citations output, which carries both `answer` and `documents`.

recipes.makeItYours:
- Use any chat model on the **LLM** node. Run the grounding check above on a few answers to see how well your model cites.
- Write your own instructions in place of the citation instructions, but keep the numbered form `[1]`: that is what Extract Citations resolves first. It also accepts a chunk id in brackets, such as `[kbc_...]`.
- Lower `topK` (4 in the sample) to keep the prompt short, or add a **Rerank** step before the prompt: see [hybrid search and reranking](/recipes/hybrid-search-rerank).
recipes.makeItSafer:
- Retrieved chunks are outside content and can carry instructions for the model. [Content rules](/product/content-rules#outside-content-at-the-model-boundary) can check each retrieved document before it reaches the model.
- Tell readers when an answer has no citations: branch on `hasCitations` with an If node.
- Cap model spend with a [budget](/product/budgets).

recipes.title: Hybrid search and reranking for better RAG
recipes.description: Fuse BM25 keyword and vector search with reciprocal rank fusion, then rerank the top chunks, so RAG finds exact error codes and paraphrases alike.
recipes.keysNote: A rerank key (Cohere, Jina or Voyage) and an OpenAI key
recipes.whatYouGet: A RAG workflow that takes 20 candidates from keyword and vector search combined, reranks them, and answers from the best 3.
recipes.summary: **Retrieve (hybrid)** searches a built-in knowledge base two ways at once: BM25 keyword search and vector search, 50 candidates each. It merges the two lists with reciprocal rank fusion and keeps the top 20. **Rerank** sends those 20 to a hosted reranking model (Cohere as shipped), which scores each chunk against the question and keeps the best 3. The **Grounded Prompt** and **LLM** answer from those. As shipped it needs a Cohere key for the rerank and an OpenAI key for the embedder and the model. Without them you can still compare the search modes with the demo embedder.
steps: Create a knowledge base and add documents, as in the [knowledge base recipe](/recipes/rag-knowledge-base#create-a-knowledge-base-with-the-api), with the embedder the **Retrieve (hybrid)** node uses (`openai-embedder` as shipped). Open **Retrieve (hybrid)** and pick it under **Knowledge Base** (or put its id in place of `<your-kb-id>` in the JSON file).

Store your Cohere key as a [secret](/security/secrets). Open **Rerank** and pick it under **Reranker API Key Secret**. Or delete `secretRef` from the file and set `COHERE_API_KEY` on the server. For Jina or Voyage, change `providerId`, `model` and the key.
Run it and open **Retrieve (hybrid)** and **Rerank** in the run to compare their order.

sections.heading: Why hybrid
sections.body:
Vector search matches meaning: "I forgot my login" finds a chunk about resetting a password. It is weaker on exact strings such as error codes, product ids and rare names. Keyword search is the reverse. Hybrid runs both and merges the two ranked lists with reciprocal rank fusion (RRF): each list gives a chunk `1 / (k + rank)`, and the sums decide the order. A chunk near the top of both lists wins. The sample uses `k = 60`, the constant from the paper that introduced RRF, which found it near-optimal but not critical.

Hybrid and `bm25` modes work only with the built-in knowledge base. With an external vector store the node falls back to vector search without an error. If keyword search finds no chunk at all, hybrid returns the vector results unchanged.

sections.heading: What a run does
sections.body:
We ran the sample on a fresh install with no provider keys, against a knowledge base holding a short helpdesk FAQ in 4 chunks, one of them about error code E1042.

**As shipped**, the run stops at the first step that needs a key. With `openai-embedder` and no key, that is **Retrieve**: `OpenAI Embedding API error: Unauthorized`. With the `token-embedder` demo embedder, retrieval succeeds and **Rerank** stops: `Reranker "cohere" requires an API key — pass via secretRef or set COHERE_API_KEY`. Note that while the node holds a `secretRef`, even a placeholder one, it uses only that secret and never reads `COHERE_API_KEY`. Delete the `secretRef` to use the environment key.

**The search modes, compared.** We removed the Rerank node and ran the retrieve step in each mode with `topK: 3`:

| Question | `vector` | `bm25` | `hybrid` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What does E1042 mean? | E1042 chunk first, then billing, then reset | the E1042 chunk only | E1042 chunk first (both rankers), then billing, then reset |
| How do I reset my password? | reset chunk first | the reset chunk only | reset chunk first (both rankers) |

Keyword search returns only chunks that share a word with the question; vector search always fills `topK`. In hybrid mode each chunk records which rankers found it (`retrieval.rankers`) and its `rrfScore`: 0.0328 for a chunk ranked first by both (2/61), 0.0161 and 0.0159 for chunks only vector search found (1/62, 1/63). With 4 small chunks the order barely moves. Hybrid matters more on larger collections, where an exact code can sit far down a vector ranking; measure it on yours (below).

**The rerank step was not observed**, as we had no rerank key. From the code: Rerank sends the question and the text of each upstream chunk to the provider (Cohere's `top_n` is `topN`), keeps the order the provider returns, and adds `rerankerScore` and `reranker: { providerId, model }` to each chunk's metadata. It returns `documents`, a numbered `context` and the same `citationInstructions` as Retrieve. With no upstream chunks it returns an empty list and makes no call. A provider error fails the run with the provider's status, such as `Cohere rerank 401: ...`.

sections.heading: Measure the difference
sections.body: Do not take hybrid or a reranker on faith: measure them on your own questions. Build a few fixtures (a question and the answer you expect), then score each variant with `context_precision` (how much of what was retrieved is relevant) and `context_recall` (how much of the expected answer the retrieved text covers). Both are programmatic and free per fixture. They read `documents` from the run's output, and this sample's output is only the answer text, so evaluate a copy that ends at the step you are measuring, **Retrieve (hybrid)** or **Rerank**. See [RAG-specific eval scorers](/nodes/knowledge-bases#rag-specific-eval-scorers-phase-9-5) and [golden sets](/product/golden-sets) for running them on every change.

recipes.makeItYours: - Tune the fusion under **Advanced** on the retrieve node while **Search Mode** is hybrid: **Candidates per Ranker** (`candidatesPerRanker`), **Vector Weight** and **Keyword Weight** (`vectorWeight`, `bm25Weight`) and **RRF k** (`rrfK`). See [hybrid search](/nodes/knowledge-bases#hybrid-search-phase-9-3). - Swap the reranker: `jina` (default model `jina-reranker-v2-base-multilingual`) or `voyage` (`rerank-2`), with `JINA_API_KEY` or `VOYAGE_API_KEY` or a secret. Change `model` too, or clear it to use the default: the sample's `rerank-english-v3.0` is a Cohere model and is sent as is. - The prompt asks the model to "Cite chunkIds inline", but the context numbers chunks `[1]`, `[2]`. Put `{{citationInstructions}}` in the prompt instead and add an Extract Citations step: see [RAG with citations](/recipes/rag-with-citations).
recipes.makeItSafer:
- A reranker is one more service that receives your documents' text. Keep it in mind when you choose which documents to index.
- Retrieved chunks can carry instructions for the model: [content rules](/product/content-rules#outside-content-at-the-model-boundary) can check them before they reach the model.
- The rerank provider bills you directly, and L2M budgets do not count rerank calls. Cap the model side with a [budget](/product/budgets).
