recipes.title: Extract structured JSON from text with an LLM
recipes.description: Turn free text into JSON that matches a schema with the Output Parser node, retry when the model's JSON is invalid, and use the fields in later steps.
recipes.keysNote: A model: local Ollama as shipped, or a provider key
recipes.whatYouGet: A workflow that asks a model for a sentiment label and returns it as checked JSON: `{"name": ..., "sentiment": "positive"}`.
recipes.summary: A **System Prompt** tells the model to answer only with JSON that has `name` and `sentiment` fields. The **LLM Call** answers the text from **Text Input**, and the **Output Parser** reads the answer as JSON and checks it against a schema: both fields required, `sentiment` one of `positive`, `negative` or `neutral`. If the check fails, the parser asks the same model to fix its answer, up to 2 times, and fails the run if it still does not match. As shipped, the model is `llama3.1` on a local Ollama server (`http://localhost:11434/v1`).
steps: Open the **LLM Call** node and point it at a model you have: pull `llama3.1` into Ollama, or switch the provider and store its key as a [secret](/security/secrets). In Docker, `localhost` is the container: use `http://host.docker.internal:11434/v1` for Ollama on the host. On Linux that name resolves only if the `api` service has `extra_hosts: ["host.docker.internal:host-gateway"]`, which the repo's `docker-compose.yml` does not set. Save.
Run it, then open the run and click **Output Parser** to see `parsed`, `retries` and `parserTrace`.
Change the text on **Text Input** and run it again.

sections.heading: What a run does
sections.body: We did not run the sample against Ollama. We ran it with the echo model and with a small local stand-in server that returns fixed answers, to see each parser path: | The model answered | Result | | --- | --- | | `{"name": "product review", "sentiment": "positive"}` | Success, `retries: 0`, strategy `json_parse` | | The same JSON inside a ```` ```json ```` block, after "Here is the result:" | Success, `retries: 0` | | `"sentiment": "very happy"`, then valid JSON on the retry | Success, `retries: 1` | | `"sentiment": "very happy"` every time | Run fails: `Output Parser failed after 2 retries: Field 'sentiment' value 'very happy' not in enum: positive, negative, neutral` | | "The sentiment is clearly positive." every time | Run fails: `Output Parser failed after 2 retries: Invalid JSON (strict): ...` | Each retry is a separate call to the same model, with the system prompt "You are a JSON formatting assistant. Output ONLY valid JSON." and a message that names the error, the schema and the original answer. Retries cost tokens like any other call. With **echo**, the run fails, and it is worth knowing why. Echo's answer is the prompt, not JSON, so the parser retries, and echo repeats the correction message back. That message contains the schema, which is a JSON object, so the parser finds it, and rejects it: `Missing required field: name`. The parser looks for JSON anywhere in the text, so prose that quotes JSON can parse to something you did not mean. On success, the **Output** node's `{{parsed}}` renders the object as a JSON string: `{"name":"product review","sentiment":"positive"}`.

sections.heading: What the schema check covers
sections.body:
In `json_schema` mode the parser checks the top level of the object only: each field in `required` is present, a field typed `string`, `number` or `boolean` has that type, and a field with `enum` holds one of the listed values. Nested objects, arrays, `integer` and formats are not checked. For a full JSON Schema check, add an **Output Guardrail** node with the **Matches a JSON Schema** check and a schema, or an answer schema [output check](/product/content-rules-output-checks#answer-schema). Both are optional.

The LLM Call node does not ask the provider for a JSON mode; the JSON comes from the system prompt. That is why the parser and its retries are there.

sections.heading: When parsing fails
sections.body:
Set **Parsing Strictness** (`parsingMode`) on the parser:

- `strict` (default): the answer, a fenced block in it, or the first complete object in it must be valid JSON.
- `lenient`: also repairs common slips such as single quotes, trailing commas, unquoted keys and Python literals.
- `anything_goes`: also reads simple `key: value` lines. When parsing or the schema check still fails after the retries, the run does not fail: the parser returns `parsed: null` and a `warning`. We saw this with the prose answer above, so check for `null` before you use the result.

`parserTrace` in the node output lists each strategy tried and why it failed. See [Output Parser fails with Invalid JSON](/troubleshooting/common-issues#output-parser-fails-with-invalid-json-even-though-response-includes-json).

sections.heading: Use the result downstream
sections.body: Later nodes read the fields by path. With the Output template set to `Sentiment: ` followed by `{{parsed.sentiment}}`, our run returned `Sentiment: positive`. To route on a field, put an If node after the parser with a condition such as `{{ parsed.sentiment === "negative" }}`: see [branch a workflow on an LLM result](/recipes/branch-on-llm-output).

recipes.makeItYours:
- Edit the schema on the parser (a JSON string in **JSON Schema (Required for strict mode)**) and the system prompt together: name the same fields and values in both.
- Set **Parser Mode** to **Item List** (`item_list`) for a plain list, one item per line, returned as `items` and `count`.
- Set **LLM Max Auto-Retries** (`maxRetries`) to 1 to limit the extra calls, or to 0 to fail at once without asking the model again.
recipes.makeItSafer:
- Treat parsed fields as untrusted input, especially when the source text came from outside: validate them before they reach a database, a shell or a URL.
- Cap model spend, retries included, with a [budget](/product/budgets).

recipes.title: Branch a workflow on an LLM result
recipes.description: Send a webhook payload through a model, test the answer with an If node, and route it to one of two outputs. Plus what to do when the model call fails.
recipes.keysNote: None: runs on the built-in Echo model; a provider key for real answers
recipes.whatYouGet: A webhook workflow that asks a model, checks the answer with an If node, and returns either the answer or "No answer generated".
recipes.summary: A **Webhook Input** at `POST /webhook/conditional-demo` passes `user_prompt`, `system_prompt` and `session_id` from the request body to an **LLM Call**. The **Check Answer** If node tests `{{answer}}`: if the model said anything, the **Success Output** returns it; if not, the **Error Output** returns "No answer generated". Only one output runs. As shipped, the model is the built-in Echo model, which answers with the prompt it gets and needs no key, and the webhook has no authentication.
steps: Keep the built-in Echo model to check the branching first. For real answers, open the **LLM Call** node, pick a provider in the **Provider** list, set the model (**Load models** lists what the provider offers) and, for a hosted provider, its key, then save. For Ollama in Docker, use `http://host.docker.internal:11434/v1` for Ollama on the host (on Linux, add `extra_hosts: ["host.docker.internal:host-gateway"]` to the `api` service).

Send a request:

   ```bash
   curl -X POST http://localhost:4000/webhook/conditional-demo \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"user_prompt": "Is order 1042 late?"}'
   ```
Open the run and click **Check Answer** to see `evaluatedValue` and which branch it took.

sections.heading: What a run does
sections.body:
We ran it on a fresh install with the echo model and with a local stand-in server:

- **Echo.** The webhook answered `{"output":{"result":"Echo: Is order 1042 late?"}}`. Check Answer evaluated to that text, took the `true` branch, and the Error Output was marked **skipped**.
- **No `user_prompt` in the body.** Echo still answers, with a hint: "Echo provider received no user message. Wire a Text Input or Prompt Template into this LLM Call to see the echo." The true branch ran. A real model would get an empty message instead.
- **An empty answer.** With a stand-in model that returns an empty string, the run took the `false` branch and returned `{"output":{"result":"No answer generated"}}`.
- **The model is down.** With the model's server unreachable, the run failed at the LLM Call after 4 attempts, the If node never ran, and the caller got HTTP 400 with `{"output":null,"error":"openai_compatible request failed after 4 attempt(s): fetch failed"}`. The message names the node's provider; our stand-in used `openai_compatible`.

So the false branch catches an empty answer, which is rare with a working model. A model error, a bad key or a timeout fails the run before the If node. Handle those with an error workflow (below).

sections.heading: Write a better condition
sections.body: The If node renders its condition as a template and reads the result as text. It is false when the text is empty, `false`, `0`, `null` or `undefined`, and true otherwise. That is why `{{answer}}` means "the model said something". A condition with text outside its braces is one JavaScript expression: each `{{ }}` is replaced by its value, so `{{score}} > 90` compares a number and `{{answer}} === 'yes'` compares text. Quote text you compare with, since `{{status}} == done` is not an expression and fails the If node. The editor's preview under the condition shows `true` or `false` for the last run's data. A condition can also be a JavaScript expression, run in a sandbox. With `{{ answer.toLowerCase().includes("late") }}`, "Is order 1042 late?" took the true branch and "Where is order 1042?" the false one. Two habits make conditions sturdier: - **Ask the model for a label, not prose.** Tell it to answer with one word, such as `refund` or `question`, or parse JSON first with an Output Parser and test `{{parsed.intent}}`. See [extract structured JSON](/recipes/structured-output-json). - **Use a Switch node for more than two paths.** It compares one value with a list of cases and routes to the first match, or to `default`.

sections.heading: Handle failures with an error workflow
sections.body:
Build a second workflow that starts with an **Error Trigger**. Then open this workflow, choose **Error workflow…** in the editor's **⋯** menu, pick the second workflow and save (in JSON this is `"settings": { "errorWorkflowId": "<its id>" }`). When a run fails, L2M starts it with the failed run's details: `source_workflow_id`, `source_workflow_name`, `execution_id`, `error`, `error_stack` and `timestamp`.

We tested it with an error workflow whose HTTP Request step posts those fields to a local server. With the model down, it received `{"wf":"Conditional Branching Flow","err":"openai_compatible request failed after 4 attempt(s): fetch failed","exec":"..."}`. The caller of the webhook still gets the 400 error; the error workflow runs on the side, for alerts or clean-up.

recipes.makeItYours:
- Write the system prompt on the LLM Call node instead of taking `system_prompt` from the request, so callers cannot rewrite the model's instructions.
- Replace the two Output nodes with real work on each branch: a reply on one, a ticket or an approval on the other. End with a **Merge / Join** node if the branches should meet again.
recipes.makeItSafer:
- Secure the webhook before anyone else can reach it: a bearer token or an HMAC signature, and idempotency for retried calls. See [Secure webhooks](/security/secure-webhooks).
- A model's answer is untrusted text. Branch on a fixed label, not on free text that a caller can steer.
- Cap what callers can spend with a [budget](/product/budgets).

recipes.title: Use Azure OpenAI in a self-hosted workflow
recipes.description: Call an Azure OpenAI deployment from an L2M workflow, with the API key stored as an encrypted secret and only its id in the workflow file.
recipes.keysNote: An Azure OpenAI resource, deployment and key
recipes.whatYouGet: A workflow that sends a prompt to your Azure OpenAI deployment, with the key held by L2M's secret store, never in the workflow.
recipes.summary: A **Text Input** and a **Prompt Template** build the prompt, the **Azure OpenAI Chat Model** node sends it to your deployment, and the **Output** returns the answer. The node has fields for the resource endpoint, the deployment name, the API version (`2024-10-21` as shipped) and the key, which is a reference to a stored secret. The workflow file holds only the secret's id. You need an Azure OpenAI resource with a chat deployment; there is no keyless way to run this one.
steps: Store the key as a secret. In the node's config, open **Azure OpenAI Secret** and choose **+ Add New Credential...** (the provider is already set to Azure OpenAI), name it and paste the key. Or use the API (below).

On the **Azure OpenAI Chat Model** node, set **Endpoint** to `https://<your-resource>.openai.azure.com`, **Deployment** to your deployment's name (not the model's name, unless you named it after the model) and pick the secret under **Azure OpenAI Secret**. Save.
Run it. The answer is in the run's output as `result`.

sections.heading: Store the key as a secret
sections.body:
```bash
# An API key with builder rights, from Settings → Account → API Keys.
curl -X POST http://localhost:4000/api/secrets \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $L2M_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name": "azure-openai-prod", "provider": "azure_openai", "value": "<your-azure-openai-key>", "projectId": "<your-project>"}'
```

The answer holds the secret's `id` (`sec_...`) and never the value; no API returns the value again. It is encrypted at rest with AES-256-GCM under `SECRET_MASTER_KEY_BASE64`. Without `projectId` the secret lands in the default project and the answer carries a warning saying so. See [Secrets](/security/secrets).

The value can be the raw key, or JSON such as `{"apiKey": "..."}` (or `accessToken`). L2M sends it in the `api-key` header. A value with three dot-separated parts, or starting with `Bearer `, is sent as `Authorization: Bearer ...` instead, for Microsoft Entra ID tokens. L2M does not fetch or refresh such tokens itself.

sections.heading: What a run does
sections.body:
We had no Azure resource, so we ran the sample two ways on a fresh install.

**As shipped**, the run fails at the Azure node: `Provider azure_openai requires an API key via secretRef or AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY.` The placeholder secret id does not exist, and a missing secret does not fail on its own: the node falls back to the server's `AZURE_OPENAI_API_KEY`. If that is set, a workflow with a wrong secret id quietly uses the server's key.

**Against a local stand-in** for the Azure endpoint, with a stored secret, the node sent one request to `POST /openai/deployments/gpt-4o-mini/chat/completions?api-version=2024-10-21` with the key in the `api-key` header. The body held the prompt as the only message (the sample has no System Prompt node, so no system message is sent), `temperature: 0.2`, `max_tokens: 1024` and `stream: true` with `stream_options.include_usage`. The answer came back as `result`, and the node recorded the token usage the endpoint reported. With a key the endpoint refused, the run failed with `Provider azure_openai stream request failed (401): ...` and the endpoint's own message.

A real Azure endpoint was not called, so this page does not show Azure's own errors, content filtering or quotas.

sections.heading: Costs
sections.body: Workflow runs record tokens for Azure calls but no cost: the built-in price list has no Azure prices for runs, so Azure spend does not count toward a USD [budget](/product/budgets). To price it, add your deployment to `LLM_PRICING_OVERRIDES_JSON` under the provider id `azure_openai` (`azure-openai` is read the same way), keyed by the deployment name, for example `{"azure_openai":{"gpt-4o-mini":{"inputUsdPer1M":0.15,"outputUsdPer1M":0.6}}}` (use your contract's prices). Known limit: a [replay](/product/replay-and-release-gate)'s live Azure calls are recorded under the node's `model` field, not the deployment name, so price them under that name too if the two differ.

sections.heading: Serve the deployment to other apps (optional)
sections.body: The node calls Azure directly from the workflow. To let applications outside L2M use the same deployment with L2M's client tokens, budgets and audit, add a route on the [/v1 AI gateway](/product/ai-gateway): provider `azure_openai`, the deployment name as the upstream model, your endpoint as the base URL and the same stored secret as the key. Apps then call `POST /v1/chat/completions` with a public model name. Unlike workflow runs, `/v1` traffic to a deployment named `gpt-4o` or `gpt-4o-mini` is priced by default. The gateway is off until you add a route set.

recipes.makeItYours:
- Add a **System Prompt** node before the Azure node; it reads `system_prompt`.
- Use the same node as the chat model of an agent, on its `chat_model` port.
- For embeddings, use the **Embeddings Azure OpenAI** node or the `azure-openai-embedder` in RAG Retrieve.
recipes.makeItSafer:
- Keep one secret per environment and per project, and share a default-project secret with other projects only on purpose: see [project scope](/security/secrets#project-scope).
- Restrict which deployments workflows may call with a [model allowlist](/security/model-allowlists).

recipes.title: Branded PDF inventory report with charts and MCP
recipes.description: Import a workflow that reads a brand from a web page with a model, counts records from an MCP tool, draws three charts and prints a branded PDF.
recipes.keysNote: A model key, an MCP server, Chromium and a Python sandbox
recipes.whatYouGet: A two-page A4 PDF in a website's colors and logo, with three charts of records counted from an MCP tool's answer.
recipes.summary: One **Manual Trigger** starts two branches. The brand branch loads a URL with **Web Browse** in headless Chromium, and a **Prompt Template**, an **LLM Call** and an **Output Parser** turn the page's title, meta tags, image URLs and text into a brand kit: name, logo URL, two colors, a font and a tagline. The data branch calls a `list_keys` tool with an **MCP Tool** node, and a Python **Code Node** counts the records by cloud, by algorithm and by age. Three **Chart** nodes draw the counts as SVG, the two bar charts in the brand colors, a second Prompt Template builds one HTML page, and **PDF Output** prints it. The sample counts encryption keys, but any MCP tool that returns a JSON list works. It combines two smaller recipes: [brand extraction](/recipes/brand-extraction-web) and [PDF report with charts](/recipes/pdf-report-with-charts).
steps: Install Chromium for Playwright on the API host once: `pnpm exec playwright install chromium` from the repo root, or point `PDF_CHROMIUM_EXECUTABLE_PATH` at a Chromium you have. Web Browse and PDF Output both need it.

Let Python code run. With the default `CODE_SANDBOX_MODE=auto`, **Aggregate Keys** runs in a throwaway container when docker or podman is installed and both sandbox images are present locally. Without a container, Python code nodes are off by default and the node fails. See [code execution](/security/code-execution#code-nodes).

Point **Key manager list_keys** at your MCP server: set `connection.endpoint` to its streamable HTTP URL (`http://key-manager-mcp.internal/mcp` is a placeholder). For a token, set `connection.authType` to `bearer` and a `secretRef` to a stored [secret](/security/secrets), or register the server in the [MCP server registry](/product/mcp-server-registry) and set `registryServerId`.

Give **Distill Branding** a model: pick a stored secret with your OpenAI API key under **API Key Secret** (or set `OPENAI_API_KEY` on the API server), or switch the provider. To try it without a key, set its `providerId` to `echo` in the JSON file and import it again: the **Provider** list has no echo entry.

Set **Brand URL** to your site, or send a `user_prompt` with the run: it replaces the Text Input's URL. Run it, open the run and click **Render PDF**: `pdf.downloadUrl` holds the file as a `data:application/pdf;base64,...` URL, and the **PDF Report** output returns it as `result`.

sections.heading: What a run does
sections.body: We ran it on a local install with three stand-ins, so nothing left the machine: a brand page served on localhost (a title, an `og:image` logo, a `theme-color` tag and text naming two colors and a font), a local MCP server whose `list_keys` returned 12 keys, and a scripted OpenAI-compatible model that answered the brand prompt with one JSON object. Python ran in a container (we set `CODE_SANDBOX_PYTHON_IMAGE` to a stock `python:3-alpine` image). - **With the stand-ins**, the run took about 1.7 seconds: about 0.65 s each for Web Browse and the PDF, 0.3 s for the Python step (mostly starting the container) and 6 to 12 ms per chart. The PDF was 55,555 bytes on two A4 pages: the logo, brand name and tagline, a box with the total (12), the cloud bar chart in the page's primary color and the algorithm donut on page 1, and the age chart in the accent color on page 2. The age chart's heading was left at the foot of page 1; add `h2{break-after:avoid}.chart{break-inside:avoid}` to the template's CSS to keep headings with their charts. - **With the echo provider**, the model only repeats the prompt. The parser picked up the image list from the echoed text, so every brand field was empty: the PDF had no brand name, tagline or logo, and the bar charts used default colors. The run still succeeded, so check the brand values. - **With the MCP endpoint as shipped**, **Key manager list_keys** failed with `fetch failed` after about 8 seconds. The nodes that had not run yet, Web Browse included, were skipped, and the run ended with an error. The file name template is `{{results.brand_parse.parsed.brand}}-key-inventory-{{session_id}}.pdf`: a run with `session_id: "q4-review"` gave the stand-in's brand name followed by `-key-inventory-q4-review.pdf` (spaces in the brand name are kept), and without a session the name ends in `-.pdf`. The stand-in shows the plumbing; how well a real model fills in the brand kit depends on the model and the page.

sections.heading: How the branches meet
sections.body: A node sees the outputs of the nodes that point at it. The three Chart nodes have edges from both **Aggregate Keys** and **Parse Brand JSON**, so they wait for both branches. **Compose Branded HTML** has edges from the parser, the Python step, the Text Input and the charts, so its template can use `{{parsed.brand}}`, `{{totalKeys}}` and `{{cloudChart.svg}}`. **Render PDF** has only the HTML node as a parent, so its file name reads the brand with `{{results.brand_parse.parsed.brand}}`, which reaches any finished node. A Chart node fills in placeholders only in `specTemplate`, a JSON string, not in an inline `spec` object. The two bar charts use `specTemplate` with `{{ parsed.primaryColor || '#4c78a8' }}` as the bar color, so a missing color falls back to a default. The result must still be valid JSON: a color value with a quote in it fails the node. Each chart's `dataPath` (`byCloud`, `byAlgorithm`, `ageing`) names a list from the Python step. See the [Chart node](/nodes/chart) for the other fields.

sections.heading: The Python step
sections.body:
**Aggregate Keys** gets the MCP Tool node's output as `items[0]`: the tool's text in `tool_output`, and its `structuredContent` in `structured` when the server sends one. The script prefers `structured`, parses `tool_output` as JSON otherwise, and accepts a list or an object with a `keys` list. It reads each record's `algorithm`, `labels.cloud` (or `cloud`) and `createdAt`. Missing values count as `unknown`, and a record without a readable date counts as under 30 days old.

A Python code node returns what the script assigns to `result`; `log()` only adds a line to `code_logs`. Here `result` is a dictionary (`byCloud`, `byAlgorithm`, `ageing`, `totalKeys`, `generatedAt`), and its keys also appear at the top level for the next nodes. `generatedAt` goes into the report as a raw ISO timestamp; format it in the script if you want a plain date.

sections.heading: Outbound requests and untrusted input
sections.body:
Web Browse loads the page and everything it pulls in, and PDF Output loads whatever the HTML references, here the logo URL. Both go through L2M's [outbound URL checks](/security/outbound-url-checks): cloud metadata and link-local addresses are always refused, while private ranges and localhost are allowed by default, which is why our localhost page worked.

The brand values come from a web page through a model and go into the HTML without escaping, and Chromium renders that HTML with scripts on. Treat the brand URL as untrusted input. The counts have no model in their path: the charts come straight from the tool's answer.

recipes.makeItYours:
- Count something else: change the tool name and `argsTemplate` on the MCP Tool node, then the field names in the Python step. Keep the `byCloud`, `byAlgorithm` and `ageing` names, or change each chart's `dataPath`.
- Skip the model: delete the four brand nodes and put fixed colors in the chart specs and the HTML template.
- Let a chat follow up on a report: the [two-turn report and code helper](/recipes/two-turn-report-helper) saves a report per session and writes a script from it on the next turn.
recipes.makeItSafer:
- If people you do not control choose the brand URL, turn on `OUTBOUND_DENY_PRIVATE` (off by default): see [outbound URL checks](/security/outbound-url-checks#configuration).
- Keep Python in the container sandbox, not on the host: see [code execution](/security/code-execution#python-on-the-host).
- Give the workflow an MCP token that can only read. An optional [MCP tool policy](/glossary/mcp-tool-policy) can also refuse tools you did not mean to allow.
- The PDF is stored with the run as base64, so anyone who can read the run can read the report.

recipes.title: Two-turn report and code helper with session artifacts
recipes.description: Import a chat workflow that remembers artifacts between turns, routes follow-up intents and returns a PDF or code help on request.
recipes.keysNote: A model with tool calling (local Ollama as shipped) and an MCP server
recipes.whatYouGet: A chat endpoint that builds a PDF report from MCP data on one turn, saves it for the session, and writes a Python script from that saved report on a later turn.
recipes.summary: A **Webhook Input** at `POST /webhook/two-turn-report-code-helper` takes a `user_prompt` and a `session_id`. **Session Artifact Load** reads the report saved earlier in that session, if any. An **Agent Orchestrator** with a chat model, a **Simple Memory** and every tool of one MCP server answers with one JSON object: `status`, `intent`, `final_html`, `python_code`, `follow_up_question`, `chart_data` and `artifact_context`. An **Output Parser** checks it, and a **Chat Intent Router** picks a branch. A report turn prints `final_html` to PDF, saves the report with **Session Artifact Save** and returns it with the PDF attached. A code turn returns the script. Anything else returns a message. As shipped, the chat model is `qwen2.5:7b` on a local Ollama server, the MCP endpoint is a placeholder, and the webhook has no authentication.
steps: Point **Chat Model** at a model that can call tools and keep to a JSON format: pull `qwen2.5:7b` into Ollama, or switch the provider and pick a stored key. To check the plumbing without a model, set its `providerId` to `echo` in the JSON file and import it again (the **Provider** list has no echo entry). Echo never calls a tool.

Point **MCP Tools** at your MCP server: set `connection.endpoint` to its streamable HTTP URL (`http://127.0.0.1:7001/mcp` is a placeholder). `toolName: "__all__"` gives the agent every tool the server lists. For a token, set `connection.authType` to `bearer` and a `secretRef`, or register the server in the [MCP server registry](/product/mcp-server-registry) and set `registryServerId`.
Install Chromium for Playwright for the PDF: `pnpm exec playwright install chromium` from the repo root, or set `PDF_CHROMIUM_EXECUTABLE_PATH`.

Ask for a report, with a session id:

   ```bash
   curl -X POST http://localhost:4000/webhook/two-turn-report-code-helper \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"user_prompt": "Build a PDF report of our keys by cloud", "session_id": "team-a-1"}'
   ```
Ask for the code in the same session: send `"user_prompt": "Now give me a Python script that regenerates it nightly without AI"` with the same `session_id`.

Read `output.result`. A report turn has the PDF in `attachments` (`filename`, `sizeBytes` and a `data:` URL in `downloadUrl`). A code turn has `{ language, source }` in `codes`. When the agent needs more, `status` is `needs_more_info` and `follow_up_question` says what.

sections.heading: What a run does
sections.body:
We ran it on a local install with two stand-ins: a local MCP server whose one tool, `list_keys`, returned 12 keys, and a scripted OpenAI-compatible model written to follow the system prompt. A real model's answers depend on the model.

**Turn 1**, "Build a PDF report of our keys by cloud", session `t1`. The Load node found nothing. The agent was offered `session_cache_list`, `session_cache_get`, `agent_clarify` and `http_mcp__list_keys`, called `list_keys`, then answered with a report object. The parser accepted it, and the router took the agent's own `intent: "report"`. **PDF Output** printed a one-page A4 file, `mcp-report-t1.pdf` (15,717 bytes), the Save node stored five fields as `latest_report`, and the reply carried the PDF in `attachments`. The run took about 0.7 seconds.

**Turn 2**, "Now give me a Python script that regenerates it nightly without AI", same session. The Load node found the report, and the agent's prompt held it as JSON. Memory added the first turn's question and answer, but not the tool result (**Persist Tool Messages** is off). The agent called no tool and answered with `intent: "code"`; the reply carried the script in `codes`, and the PDF and Save nodes were skipped.

**A new session asking for code** had no saved report, so the stand-in returned `status: "needs_more_info"` with a question, as the system prompt asks.

**With the echo provider**, the agent's answer is its own prompt. The parser asked once more (`maxRetries: 1`), then gave `parsed: null`, and the router fell back to keywords: "report" picked the report branch. The PDF held only the request text, and every field of the saved report was null. On the router, `intentSource: "explicit"` means the agent's intent was used, `keyword` means the fallback matched a keyword, and `default` means nothing matched.

sections.heading: Memory, artifacts and the tool cache
sections.body:
The workflow keeps three things per session, under the namespace `two-turn-report-code-helper`:

- **Memory**: the last 20 messages (`maxMessages`), what the user asked and what the agent answered.
- **The artifact**: one exact JSON value under the key `latest_report`, which the next turn sees word for word instead of a summary. Each report turn replaces it.
- **The session tool cache**: each tool result from the agent's turns. With a `session_id`, the agent gets `session_cache_list` and `session_cache_get`, so it can reuse an earlier `list_keys` answer. In our runs each report turn stored one `list_keys` entry for its session.

All three need a `session_id`; without one, nothing is loaded or saved. They stay in the L2M database until you set `AGENT_MEMORY_RETENTION_DAYS` (by default they are kept): see [data retention](/operations/data-retention#what-each-setting-deletes) and [agent memory](/learn/agents/agent-memory).

sections.heading: How the router decides
sections.body: The **Chat Intent Router** reads `parsed.intent` first: `report`, `code`, `message` or a synonym such as `pdf` or `python`. If that is missing, it searches the request for its keywords: code words (`python`, `script`, `nightly` ...) beat report words (`report`, `pdf`, `chart` ...), and neither means a message. With `requireArtifactForCode` on, a code request with no saved report takes a fourth branch, `missing_context`. The sample does not wire it, and with nothing there the run ends with no output, so add a reply node first. The router finds the report through `artifactPath`, `results.load_report_artifact.latest_report`, because its own input comes from the parser.

sections.heading: What to check before you rely on it
sections.body:
The agent writes `final_html`, and Chromium renders it with scripts on; the URLs it loads go through the [outbound URL checks](/security/outbound-url-checks). The agent also writes the Python script. The prompt asks for direct REST calls, secrets from environment variables and no invented endpoints, but treat the script as a draft and read it before you run it.

If the MCP server is down, the run does not fail. With our server stopped, the agent saw only the three built-in tools, its `list_keys` call came back as `Tool 'list_keys' does not exist`, and it answered without data. Check `_mcpTools` on the Agent node when a report comes back empty.

recipes.makeItYours:
- Use your own data: the prompt names no product, so any MCP server with read tools works. Edit its report rules to name the tools and fields you want.
- Change what is kept: edit the Save node's `fields` list, and the next turn sees exactly those.
- Build the report from fixed nodes instead of model-written HTML: the [branded PDF inventory report](/recipes/key-inventory-pdf-report) draws charts from an MCP tool's answer with no model in the data path.
recipes.makeItSafer:
- Secure the webhook before anyone else can reach it, with a bearer token or an HMAC signature: see [webhook auth modes](/security/secure-webhooks#webhook-auth-modes).
- The agent gets every tool the server lists. Give it a token that can only read, and optionally hold tool calls for a person: see [human approval for agent tool calls](/guides/human-approval-for-agent-tool-calls).
- Turn on `OUTBOUND_DENY_PRIVATE` (off by default) so model-written HTML cannot load internal URLs: see [outbound URL checks](/security/outbound-url-checks#configuration).
- Cap spend with a workflow [budget](/product/budgets).
